Vereda do Forte de São Sebastião
Impasse do Forte de São Sebastião

name: Rua de Roberto Ivens
notes: Rua de Roberto Ivens is a street in Funchal north of the Municipal Garden. It was named after the explorer Roberto Ivens by council decision in 1885.

name: Rocha Furada
notes: Rocha Furada is a large natural opening in the rocks of Ponta do Furado, at Ponta de São Lourenço, Madeira. It resembles a great doorway.

name: Lapa do Sol
notes: Lapa do Sol is a scenic viewpoint near Monte Mendonho in the mountains of São Vicente, Madeira.

name: Capelas de Santa Maria Madalena
notes: The Capelas de Santa Maria Madalena are the chapels dedicated to Saint Mary Magdalene in Madeira. They are the ruined Manueline chapel at Madalena in Santo António parish, Funchal; one at Florenças in Arco da Calheta; and an old chapel in Porto Moniz that serves as a curacy seat and pilgrimage centre.

name: Pico da Terceira Lombada
notes: The Pico da Terceira Lombada is a mountain peak in the parish of Ponta Delgada, Madeira, offering fine views.

name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora da Consolação
notes: The Capelas de Nossa Senhora da Consolação are four Madeiran chapels dedicated to Our Lady of Consolation. They stand at the Ornelas entailed estate in Caniço, in Santa Luzia (Funchal) and at Foro in Estreito de Câmara de Lobos; a former one stood in Arco da Calheta.

name: Matadouro Municipal
notes: The Matadouro Municipal is Funchal's municipal slaughterhouse, opened in 1941. The entry traces the history of the city's slaughterhouses and meat markets from the fifteenth century onwards.

name: Capelas das Almas Pobres
notes: A small rock-cut chapel of the Almas Pobres in Funchal, standing between the convents of Santa Clara and Mercês. It was built in 1781 by Roque José de Araujo and is tied to a local legend about the souls in purgatory. The Elucidário also mentions an older chapel of the same name in Santa Maria Maior parish, founded around 1470.

name: Cais em frente da entrada da Cidade
notes: The quay at the Entrada da Cidade in Funchal. A municipal stone quay begun there in 1843 failed. The state later built a quay, completed in 1892, and its extension was inaugurated in 1933.

name: Cortina da Cidade
notes: The Cortina da Cidade was the circuit of walls that defended Funchal by land and sea. It was begun under D. Sebastião and completed in 1689. The Elucidário traces its construction and financing, and the gradual demolition of the walls and their gates in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

name: Capelas de São Sebastião
notes: Chapels dedicated to Saint Sebastian in Ponta do Sol, Porto Santo, Santa Cruz and São Jorge. The Elucidário gives brief notes on them, including their rebuilding in the eighteenth century.

name: Largo ou Praça dos Lavradores
notes: A square in Funchal on the left bank of the João Gomes stream. It was formerly the site of a Saturday fair selling poles and stakes for vine trellises. The main entrance of the Mercado dos Lavradores, opened in 1939, is on the square.

name: Capelas de São João Baptista
notes: Chapels dedicated to St John the Baptist in Madeira. Chief among them is the fifteenth-century São João da Ribeira chapel in Funchal, an early seat of the Franciscans. The Elucidário adds shorter notes on chapels of the same dedication in Ponta do Sol, Câmara de Lobos, Calheta, Campanário and Santana.

name: Igreja
notes: A locality in Monte parish containing the parish church and the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição. Emperor Charles of Austria is buried in the parish church.

name: Igreja
notes: A locality in Quinta Grande parish. The chapel of Santo António, built in 1884 at the Quinta do Pombal, stands there.

name: Avenida de Pedro Jose de Ornelas
notes: An avenue in Funchal, formerly the Caminho da Pena. It is named after a president of the municipal council who died in 1878.

name: Convento de Nossa Senhora ds Piedade
notes: A former Franciscan convent in Madeira founded by the Genoese settler Urbano Lomelino, who left his estate entailed to finish and maintain it. After the religious orders were abolished it returned to his heirs. No trace of it now survives.

Igreja de Nossa Senhora da Piedade

name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora da Fé
notes: Two chapels dedicated to Our Lady of Faith. One was founded in São Martinho in 1668. The other was built at Porto da Cruz in the 1820s and has since vanished.

name: Capela de Nossa Senhora de Jesus
notes: The earliest known chapel of Our Lady of Jesus. It was founded in São Martinho in 1656 by João Bettencourt de Atouguia.

notes: Chapels of Our Lady of Deliverance in Caniço, Ponta do Sol, Monte, Estreito da Calheta and São Vicente. The Elucidário records their founders and dates, and notes that the Caniço chapel was a pilgrimage site.

name: Capelas de Santa Quitéria
notes: Three former chapels dedicated to Santa Quitéria in Madeira. They stood at Pico do Cardo in Santo António parish (1727), at Lombo da Estrela in Calheta (1724), and at Madalena do Mar.

name: Nossa Senhora Mãe dos Homens
notes: Nossa Senhora Mãe dos Homens is a chapel of Our Lady Mother of Men on the Caminho do Meio in the parish of Santa Maria Maior, Funchal. It was owned by the Visconde de Cacongo.

name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora dos Milagres
notes: The Elucidário entry covers two chapels dedicated to Our Lady of Miracles on Madeira. One is in Monte (1661) and the other in Ponta do Sol (1662).

name: Ponte do Furado
notes: The Ponta do Furado is a coastal projection near Ponta de São Lourenço. It bounds the Abra inlet to the east.

name: Ilhéu de Branca
notes: The Ilhéu de Branca is a small islet at the eastern end of Madeira. It lies off the northern shore of the Ponta de São Lourenço.

name: Poços da Neve
notes: The Poços da Neve were man-made pits in Madeira's mountains used to store winter hail and snow. They supplied ice for sorbets in summer and are now abandoned.

name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora da Conceição
notes: This entry surveys the chapels in Madeira dedicated to Our Lady of the Conception, from the 16th century to 1930, with their founders and dates. It includes the Capela-Monumento at Babosas, Monte, built in 1906 to mark the jubilee of the dogma of the Immaculate Conception.

name: Lombada, Ribeira e Capela de São Pedro
notes: The Lombada de São Pedro is a locality in the parish of Santa Cruz, crossed by a stream also called the Ribeira da Boaventura. The chapel of São Pedro was founded there in the early 16th century, destroyed by the flood of 1803 and rebuilt.

name: Capela de São Pedro Gonçalves Telmo
notes: The Capela de São Pedro Gonçalves Telmo was a former chapel near the beach at Calheta. The Elucidário refers the reader to the entry Corpo Santo.

name: Ponte da Fonte da Areia.
notes: The Ponta da Fonte da Areia is a small point on the north-west coast of Porto Santo, at Fonte da Areia.

name: Pico da Fonte da Bica
notes: The Pico da Fonte da Bica is a peak of 1,560 metres on the Paul da Serra plateau, Madeira.

name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora da Vida
notes: These are two chapels dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Vida in the Funchal area. One was founded by Manuel Valente in 1679 in the parish of São Pedro, though its site is unknown; the other was founded by Inês Teixeira at Fajã do Mar.

name: Nova Aldeia ou Aldeia da Rainha
notes: Nova Aldeia, or Aldeia da Rainha, was a short-lived settlement at Santo da Serra. It was founded by royal charter in 1768 for families moved there from Porto Santo.

name: Beco do Ribeirinho
notes: The Beco do Ribeirinho is an alley in Funchal linking the Travessa do Rego and the Travessa da Conveniência. In 1902 the council allowed part of it to be closed off.

name: Porto e Cais da Ribeira Brava
notes: This is the landing place of Ribeira Brava, a pebble beach where embarking was difficult. A quay was built there between 1904 and 1908, linked to the town by a tunnel and a short road and served by coastal steamers.

name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora do Amparo
notes: These are several chapels in Madeira dedicated to Our Lady of Amparo. The chief one is at Álamos (Água de Mel) in Santo António, seat of the Água de Mel entail; others stood in São Martinho, Ponta do Pargo and Machico.

name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora da Boa Viagem
notes: These are two chapels of Our Lady of Good Voyage in Funchal. One was founded in 1711 at Carne Azeda in Santa Luzia. The other is an ancient chapel in Santa Maria Maior founded by Bento da Veiga, whose adjoining house reputedly held the first customs house.

candidates.name: Mosteiro de Nossa Senhora da Encarnação do Funchal

name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora do Bom Sucesso
notes: These are three chapels of Our Lady of Good Success. One is at Garachico, straddling the boundary of Câmara de Lobos and Estreito de Câmara de Lobos; another is at Lombo da Estrela in Calheta (1683). The third, on the Caminho do Meio in Funchal, is owned by the municipal council.

name: Visconde do Ribeiro Rea
notes: Visconde do Ribeiro Rea is a square in Funchal by the Rua da Carreira, where the bishop's palace has its main entrance. It occupies the site of the old British cemetery, demolished in 1888.

name: Asilos
notes: Asilos refers to the first attempt by the Funchal Municipal Council, made before constitutional government, to found a charitable home for orphans and invalids. The attempt was unsuccessful.

name: Cais na Ilha do Porto Santo
notes: The entry records the pier serving the island of Porto Santo. It also notes a plan of 1824 for a mole and quay at the Baixas de São Tiago in Funchal, which was abandoned.

name: Boca dos Corregos
notes: Boca dos Corregos is a site at about 1300 m near Pico Grande. It overlooks Curral das Freiras and the Serra de Água valley.

name: Túmulo-Monumento
notes: The Túmulo-Monumento is a memorial in the Angústias cemetery in Funchal. It commemorates those killed by German submarine shells at Funchal on 3 December 1916 and was handed to the municipal council in 1917.

candidates.name: Monumento a Nossa Senhora da Paz

name: Necrotério
notes: The Necrotério is the mortuary at the Angústias cemetery in Funchal. It was built by order of the municipal council in 1900 to hold the bodies of the poor and the unclaimed.

name: Travessa do Nery
notes: The Travessa do Nery was a lane in the parish of Santa Maria Maior, Funchal, named after Canon Vicente Nery da Silva. It was later widened and renamed Caminho do Acciaioly.

name: Capela de São João e Santana
notes: The Capela de São João e Santana is a chapel built in 1814 by João António de Gouveia Rego at the Quinta do Trapiche in Santo António, Funchal. The house adjoining it later housed the seminary.

Igreja da Casa de Saúde de São João de Deus

name: Capela de Nossa Senhora do Pilar
notes: The Capela de Nossa Senhora do Pilar is a private chapel with a quinta at the Pilar site in São Martinho, Funchal. It was founded in 1676 by Gonçalo de Freitas Drumond.

notes: The Convent of Nossa Senhora da Incarnação in Funchal was founded in 1650 by Canon Henrique Calaça de Viveiros to celebrate Portugal's restoration of independence. Its site was later used as a British barracks, the diocesan seminary and offices of the Junta Geral.

name: Fajã das Nogueiras
notes: A locality in the uplands of Faial parish, Madeira, with a small shelter house for travellers.

name: Livramento
notes: Locality in Ponta do Sol parish, Madeira. It has a chapel of Nossa Senhora do Livramento, built in 1656 as the seat of an entail.

name: Populaçâo, Superficie e Situaçâo Geográfica da ilha do Porto Santo
notes: Statistical entry on the island of Porto Santo. It gives the island's population from 1529 to 1940, the differing estimates of its surface area, and its geographical coordinates.

name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora da Nazaré
notes: Collective entry on three Madeiran chapels dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Nazaré, in Arco da Calheta, Câmara de Lobos and São Martinho. It gives their founders and dates, and a fishermen's tradition about the lady of the entail at Câmara de Lobos.

name: Pontas
notes: List of the principal headlands (pontas) of Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas, grouped by municipality.

name: Casas de Abrigo
notes: Mountain refuge huts built in the high serras of Madeira to shelter travellers caught by storms. The Elucidário lists those existing at the time and notes their poor state and staffing.

name: Águas Doces
notes: A small beach and stretch of coast near Funchal, lying between the Ilhéu da Pontinha and the mouth of the Ribeiro Seco.

name: Águas férreas
notes: Entry on Madeira's iron-bearing springs. The chief of these is the Jamboto spring in Santo António, analysed by Carlos Lepierre in 1900.

name: Capelas de São José
notes: Survey of chapels dedicated to Saint Joseph in Madeira and Porto Santo, with their founders and dates. It covers chapels in Ribeira Brava, Calheta, Porto Santo, Machico, Santa Cruz and Camacha.

name: Praça do Município
notes: Square in Funchal, formerly the Largo do Colégio. It was created in 1836 on part of the churchyard of São João Evangelista and greatly enlarged in 1943–44.

name: Furna da Mulher
notes: A cave or sea grotto on the western coast of Deserta Grande in the Desertas Islands.

name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora da Boa Hora
notes: Entry on the chapels of Our Lady of Boa Hora. These stand at Torre (Câmara de Lobos), above Funchal (1726) and at Fajã in Arco da Calheta.

notes: Chapel of Our Lady of Boa Nova in São Gonçalo parish, Funchal, founded in 1701.

notes: A lost chapel of Santa Brígida in São Pedro parish, Funchal, founded in 1668. Its site is unknown.

name: Capelas de São Paulo
notes: Entry on the chapels dedicated to Saint Paul in Madeira. Chief among them is the ancient chapel on the Largo de São Paulo in Funchal, founded by João Gonçalves Zarco, which briefly housed the parish of São Pedro; there is also a ruined chapel at Porto Moniz.

name: Porto e Cais do Campanario
notes: A small, poor landing place on the coast of Campanário parish. A modest landing stage was built there in 1909.

Escola Básica e Secundária Padre Manuel Álvares (Campanário)

name: Capelas de São Luís
notes: The Elucidário records two chapels dedicated to São Luís. One is an early eighteenth-century chapel at Diferença in Faial. The other was built by Bishop D. Luís Figueiredo de Lemos beside the old Episcopal Palace in Funchal, and he was buried there.

name: Preces
notes: Preces is a locality in the parish of Machico, within the inhabited sítio of Marco. It is named after the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Preces, founded in 1750.

name: Posto Marítimo de Desinfecção
notes: The Posto Marítimo de Desinfecção is a small maritime disinfection station that has operated at the Pontinha in Funchal since 1901. It was funded through the Junta Geral and staffed by government-paid personnel.

name: Posto Médico Municipal
notes: The Posto Médico Municipal is the municipal medical post of Funchal, opened by the town council in 1889. It acquired an X-ray apparatus in 1922.

candidates.name: Caminho Municipal ao Sítio do Pico
Caminho Municipal ao Sítio do Pico

name: Porto e cais da Oliveira
notes: The Porto e cais da Oliveira is a small quay at Ponta da Oliveira in Caniço, built in 1909. It is linked to the main road by a branch 1,800 metres long.

name: Porto e Praia do Arco de São Jorge
notes: The Porto e Praia do Arco de São Jorge is a small, poor landing place with a short beach on the coast of the parish of Arco de São Jorge. Disembarking there is difficult.

candidates.name: Igreja do Arco de São Jorge
Junta de Freguesia do Arco de São Jorge

name: Órgão de Santa Clara
notes: The Órgão de Santa Clara is the old organ of the extinct Convent of Santa Clara in Funchal, said to have been given by the children of João Gonçalves Zarco in 1498. The Elucidário reproduces a 1924 newspaper article on its restoration, which also mentions the similar restoration of the organ of Machico parish church.

name: Moradias de Zargo
notes: The Moradias de Zargo are the successive residences of João Gonçalves Zargo in Funchal: a wooden house by the Santa Catarina chapel, a stone house near São Paulo, and a final home near the Conceição de Cima (Santa Clara) church. The author identifies this last house with the present Quinta das Cruzes, and the entry traces its later owners and the two-handed sword attributed to Zargo.

name: Baixa da Conceição.
notes: The Baixa da Conceição is a shoal near the Ilhéu da Lapa off the coast of Campanário.

name: Largo da Conceição
notes: The Largo da Conceição is a square in Funchal, commonly called Largo das Babosas. It is named after the Capela-Monumento of the Conceição, built in 1906 to mark the fiftieth anniversary of the dogma.

name: Porto e Ribeira de São Vicente
notes: The Porto e Ribeira de São Vicente comprises the small, difficult landing place at São Vicente on Madeira's north coast and the São Vicente stream. At the stream's mouth stands a chapel on a basalt rock, and there is a lava cave nearby.

name: Capelas de São Francisco
notes: The Elucidário gives notes on three chapels dedicated to St Francis: in Calheta, in São Pedro (São Francisco das Furnas) and in Santa Luzia.

candidates.name: Capela de São João da Ribeira

name: Capelas de São Francisco Xavier
notes: The Elucidário records chapels of St Francis Xavier in Calheta (1693), Santa Cruz (1684) and Porto da Cruz.

name: Rua do Chapéu
notes: Rua do Chapéu is the former name of a stretch of the present Rua Correia Heredia in Funchal, between Rua da Figueira Preta and Rua do Bom Jesus.

name: Enseada e Porto do Lugar de Baixo
notes: A small cove and beach landing place at Lugar de Baixo. It was sometimes better for landing than the quays of Ponta do Sol and Ribeira Brava. Infante D. Luís landed there in 1858.

name: Igreja de Nossa Senhora do Carmo
notes: The Carmo church in Funchal was built in 1656–1660 for the Third Order of Carmel and gave its name to its street. It contains the only artistically notable mausoleums on the island.

candidates.name: Capela de Nossa Senhora do Amparo
Capela de Nossa Senhora do Amparo

name: Ferreiros
notes: Rua dos Ferreiros is one of Funchal's busiest streets, running from Rua 5 de Outubro to the Torreão bridge. It was earlier known by the names Peru, Estudo and Pinheiro, and was renamed Rua do Comércio in 1915.

name: Calhau e Porto da Aldonça
notes: A small landing place with a short beach on the coast of Gaula parish.

name: Capelas de Santo António
notes: A survey of the chapels dedicated to Saint Anthony across Madeira, from the 16th to the early 20th century. For each chapel it gives the parish, founder, date of construction or blessing and later fate, whether surviving, rebuilt or vanished.

name: Farolim do Ilhéu
notes: A small fixed-light beacon on the islet at Funchal harbour, popularly known as 'a brasa do ilhéu'. It was in service from 1866 until it was replaced in 1931.

candidates.name: Ilhéu do Forte de Nossa Senhora da Conceição

name: Fajãzinha de Bento
notes: A locality in the parish of Serra de Água where Funchal Municipal Council owned a small property, which was sold in 1918.

name: Baixa, Enseada e Porto dos Barbeiros
notes: The Barbeiros shoal, the Enseada dos Barbeiros (also called Enseada de Guilherme) and a small landing place of the same name, on the coast of Porto Santo.

name: Muncipio do Porto do Moniz
notes: The municipality of Porto Moniz in north-western Madeira was created in 1835 after long local petitions and was repeatedly abolished and restored in the nineteenth century. Porto Moniz was never raised to the status of a vila, serving only as the seat of the concelho.

name: Casa dos Consules
notes: An 18th-century town house in Funchal, named after the consulates once housed there. It is admired for its architecture.

name: Sanatórios da Madeira
notes: Tuberculosis sanatoria at Monte, Funchal, arising from the Hohenlohe concession of 1903. The Elucidário records the diplomatic dispute that led the Portuguese State to buy back the concession in 1909. It also reproduces Dr António de Lencastre's 1903 report and a 1914 government notice leasing the confiscated properties at Monte.

name: Ribeiras
notes: General term for Madeira's streams, which rise on the central mountain range and run through deep, narrow valleys to the sea. They are torrential in winter and often dry in summer. The Elucidário describes their destructive floods and lists the island's principal streams.

name: Mercado e Capela de São Sebastião
notes: Ancient chapel of São Sebastião in Funchal, demolished in 1803 by Governor D. José Manuel da Câmara to build a market. The people rebuilt it in 1821, but it had been demolished again by 1827. Its square, now Largo do Comércio, has a marble fountain.

candidates.name: Capela de São Luís de Tolosa
Capela de São João da Ribeira

name: Cais do Ilhéu de Fora
notes: Small quay on the Ilhéu de Fora, built in 1870 for the lighthouse staff. The same entry also notes the Abra quay (1905) and the Caniçal landing stage (1909).

candidates.name: Praceta do Cais da Pedra da Eira

name: Cais do Salto do Cavalo
notes: Private quay at Salto do Cavalo, built by the industrialist Pedro da Cunha Pires.

name: Cais do “Palace Hotel”
notes: Quay of the Palace Hotel on the Estrada Monumental. The same entry also notes the Wilson Company quay near Quinta do Calaça, built around 1903.

name: Cais do Pesqueiro
notes: Landing stage at Pesqueiro, built by the Junta Geral in 1916.

name: Cumiada Alta
notes: Cumiada Alta is a high ridge on Madeira, rising above 1,700 metres near Pico Ruivo and the basalt column known as Homem em Pé. The Elucidário notes it for its rare plants.

name: Posto de Desinfecção do Campo da Barca
notes: The Posto de Desinfecção do Campo da Barca was Funchal's public disinfection station, built in 1904 and opened in 1905 by the Junta Geral. It disinfected homes and public buildings after cases of contagious disease, notably during epidemics.

name: Enseada, Porto e Cais de Machico
notes: The bay of Machico is one of the widest and most picturesque bays of the Madeira archipelago. The Elucidário describes its harbour and landing quays, recording successive quays built in 1870–1873, 1905 and 1907 and harbour lights installed in 1931.

candidates.name: Escola Básica e Secundária de Machico

name: Porto ou Portinho da Morena
notes: The Porto or Portinho da Morena is a small landing place on the south-south-west coast of Porto Santo.

name: Monumentos
notes: This is the Elucidário's introductory heading to brief notes on the few public monuments of Madeira.

name: Monumento comemorativo do Bombardeamento do Funchal
notes: This is a small memorial to the bombardment of Funchal, standing in the old Angústias cemetery.

name: Monumento aos Aviadore
notes: This monument in Funchal's Jardim Municipal commemorates the 1921 Lisbon–Funchal flight of Gago Coutinho and Sacadura Cabral.

name: Cabos
notes: This entry describes Madeira's two capes, Cabo Garajau and Cabo Girão, covering their names, geology and botanical interest.

name: Forte de S. Felipe da Praça
notes: The Forte de S. Felipe da Praça was a fort in Funchal built in 1628 by the bishop-governor D. Jerónimo Fernando. It was later sold and replaced by a warehouse.

name: Forte de Santo António da Alfândega
notes: A fort in Funchal, Madeira. It was a redoubt built in 1644–45 on the walls of the Customs House to cover the beach with crossfire. It was later converted into warehouses.

name: Forte de Loures
notes: A 17th-century fort in Funchal covering the Gonçalo Aires cove, traditionally said to have been built by a private individual. Captain-General D. Diogo Coutinho wished to establish a silk factory there.

notes: A triangular fort at Machico built in 1706 at no cost to the Crown. It was the last fort to surrender to the Miguelist landing of 1828.

name: Forte de S. Roque de Machico
notes: A fort built during the Philippine period at the mouth of the Ribeirinho in Machico bay. Only fragments of its walls remain.

name: Quedas de Água
notes: The Elucidário entry lists the best-known waterfalls on Madeira island. They are grouped by the streams and valleys where they occur.

name: Rua de Júlio da Silva Carvalho
notes: A street in Madeira named after Júlio da Silva Carvalho, with its own entry in the Elucidário.

name: Paços do Concelho
notes: The town hall of Funchal, an eighteenth-century palace on Rua do Comércio bought by the municipal council in 1883. The Elucidário also traces the many buildings the council occupied from the fifteenth century onwards. It adds brief notes on the town halls of the other Madeiran municipalities.

name: Capelas das Almas
notes: Chapels in Madeira dedicated to the Souls in Purgatory, located in Ribeira Brava, Estreito de Câmara de Lobos, Calheta and Ponta do Sol. Several of them have been lost or demolished.

name: Igrejas Inglesas
notes: The Protestant churches of Funchal. They comprise the Anglican church in Rua da Bela Vista (completed 1822), a second Anglican church in Rua dos Aranhas (1848) and the Scottish church.

name: Rua da Igrejinha
notes: A former street in Funchal running between Largo do Colégio and Rua das Pretas. It was named after the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade, known as the 'Igrejinha', which was founded in 1613 and demolished in 1836.

name: Rua dos Moinhos
notes: A former name of part of Rua das Mercês in Funchal. It was named after a mill that once stood there, and the street was originally called Rua do Peso.

name: Mirantes
notes: The Elucidário's entry on the viewpoints (mirantes or miradouros) of Madeira. It lists those in Funchal and elsewhere and recalls the viewpoints recommended by Civil Governor José Silvestre Ribeiro in 1850.

name: Vapor
notes: The 'Vapor' was a curious red wooden building spanning the Santa Luzia stream in Funchal. It was built in 1837 as a café and bathhouse and was demolished around 1898.

name: Ilha da Deserta Grande ou somente Deserta
notes: The largest of the three Desertas islands: steep, nearly flat-topped and with scant brackish water. It was never permanently inhabited but was used for hunting, orchil gathering, grazing and some cereal growing. The entry covers its geography, history and fauna, including a corsair attack in 1503 and a landslide in 1894.

name: Mercados
notes: The Elucidário's entry on Funchal's public markets, chiefly the Mercado de S. João. That market opened in 1823 on land leased from the Franciscans and was demolished in 1883 to make way for the municipal theatre.

name: Portos da Madeira
notes: A survey of the ports and landing places of the Madeira archipelago, graded as good, tolerable or poor. It notes recent improvements and includes a 1944 report on planned harbour works.

name: Capelas de Santana
notes: The Elucidário's list of chapels in Madeira dedicated to Saint Anne (Santana). It gives their parishes, founders and foundation dates where known, ranging from 1607 to 1790.

name: Ribeira de Gonçalo Aires
notes: The Gonçalo Aires stream on Madeira. It rises at Pico do Infante and carries little water.

name: Ribeira do Vigario
notes: The Vigário stream, also called Ribeira de Câmara de Lobos. It rises at Achada do Poiso.

name: Ilhéu, Porto e Ribeira de Porto da Cruz
notes: These are three coastal features of Porto da Cruz parish that share its name: an islet, a small harbour whose landing place is called Furna, and a stream that flows into the sea nearby.

name: Pico da Cruz
notes: This Pico da Cruz is one of the highest heights surrounding the parish of Serra de Água.

name: Cantim
notes: Cape Cantim is a point on the Moroccan coast at the latitude of Madeira. It is the African point closest to the archipelago, about 350 miles away.

name: Ponta, Porto e Cais da Ponta do Sol
notes: This entry describes the headland, small harbour and quay of Ponta do Sol on Madeira's south-west coast, and the possible origin of the name. The quay was built by the municipal council in 1848–1850; an extension project of 1880 was never carried out.

name: Forte do Porto da Cruz
notes: The fort of Porto da Cruz was built in 1708 and dismantled in 1804. The same entry notes the Fort of Santo António at Paul do Mar, built in 1754.

name: Forte de S. Jorge da Calheta
notes: The Fort of São Jorge was a fort at Calheta. The Elucidário briefly records its captain in 1751.

candidates.name: Escola Básica do 1º ciclo com pré-escolar da Calheta

name: Reduto de S. Jorge
notes: The Reduto de S. Jorge was a redoubt in the parish of São Jorge, Madeira. The Elucidário gives only a brief note on it, recording who its captain was in 1785.

name: Forte de S. José da Ilha do Porto Santo
notes: The Forte de S. José is a fort in the town of Porto Santo. It was built under Pombal's government and included a residence for the governors. In 1921 it was ceded to the fiscal guard.

name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora do Rosário
notes: This entry covers the chapels dedicated to Our Lady of the Rosary in several Madeiran parishes, including São Roque in Funchal. The Elucidário lists their founders and dates of foundation.

name: Capelas de Nossa Senhora da Salvação
notes: This entry covers two chapels of Our Lady of Salvation. One, at Moinhos in Caniço, was founded in 1614 and is now in ruins; the other is in Funchal.

name: Capela de Nossa Senhora da Saúde do Monte Olivete
notes: The Capela de Nossa Senhora da Saúde do Monte Olivete was a chapel in the parish of Santa Maria Maior, Funchal, which no longer exists. It was built on an entail founded by Pedro Lopes de Vasconcelos in 1675.

notes: The Capela de Nossa Senhora do Vale is a chapel at Vale Formoso, in the parish of Santa Luzia, Funchal. It was founded and endowed by António Vogado in 1726.

name: Monumento a João Gonçalves Zargo
notes: The Monumento a João Gonçalves Zargo is a bronze statue of Zargo, first captain-donatary of Funchal, by Francisco Franco. It was inaugurated on the Avenida Arriaga, Funchal, in 1934.

name: Monumento aos mortos da Grande Guerra
notes: The Monumento aos mortos da Grande Guerra is a small memorial in Funchal to those killed in the First World War. Its foundation stone was laid in 1935.

candidates.name: Monumento a Nossa Senhora da Paz

name: Monumento ao Doutor Teles
notes: The Monumento ao Doutor Teles is a modest monument in the gardens of the Asilo de Mendicidade e Órfãos, Funchal. It honours Dr Alexandre da Cunha Teles, a benefactor of charitable services, and was inaugurated in 1939.

name: Casas de Romeiros
notes: The Casas de Romeiros were pilgrims' shelters built at Monte, at Santo António da Serra and at Piedade on the Ponta de São Lourenço. The Elucidário gives notes on their history.

name: Ilhéus do Faial
notes: The Ilhéus do Faial are a group of small islets and rocks off the coast of Faial parish, Madeira, known collectively by that name.

candidates.name: Associação desportiva e cultural do Faial

name: Fajã
notes: Fajã is a Madeiran term for fertile tracts of land formed by landslides, found both inland and along the coast. The Elucidário notes that it is a common element in place-names.

name: Fajã
notes: Fajã is an inhabited locality in the parish of Santo António, Funchal, on the left bank of the Ribeira dos Socorridos.

name: Cinco de Junho
notes: Rua Cinco de Junho is a Funchal street linking Rua dos Aranhas (now Rua Dr. Chaves) with Largo do Ribeiro Real. It was opened when the old cemetery alleys were demolished, and is named after 5 June 1834, the date on which the constitutional government was proclaimed in Madeira.

name: Nomes de Ruas
notes: Nomes de Ruas is an essay on the naming of streets in Funchal. It recalls the municipal council's resolution of 19 June 1890 to name new streets after illustrious Madeirans and laments that this was seldom followed. It lists notable Madeirans still uncommemorated in 1921 and urges restraint in renaming old streets.

name: Caminho de Luis Miranda
notes: Caminho de Luís Miranda was the name, from 1896 to 1910, of the road between the parish church of Santo António and the Ribeira. It honoured Luís de Bettencourt Miranda, long-serving secretary of the Funchal council.

name: Praça do Peixe
notes: The Praça do Peixe, or Praça de São Pedro, was Funchal's fish market. It began as a small market built by the Câmara in 1817 and was replaced by a building opened in 1840, which was later demolished for the Avenida do Mar.

name: Alfândega de Machico
notes: The customs house of Machico was created by royal charter in 1477, together with those of Funchal and Santa Cruz. Although it stood at the seat of the captaincy, it was less busy than that of Santa Cruz. Its last Manueline ruins, in Rua da Árvore, were demolished in 1916.

name: Fortaleza de S. Lourenço
notes: The Fortress of São Lourenço in Funchal was begun under King Manuel I and completed under Philippine rule. It was stormed by French pirates in 1566 and later housed a chapel and various public buildings.

candidates.name: Núcleo Museológico do Palácio de São Lourenço

name: Hospital de S. Lazaro
notes: The Hospital de São Lázaro was Funchal's leper hospital, probably founded in the late fifteenth century and maintained by the Câmara. It closed in 1912, after which its building became the civil prison. The entry also records medical opinions on leprosy (elephantiasis) in Madeira.

name: Teatro de Bom Gosto
notes: The Teatro de Bom Gosto was a small theatre in Funchal, built around 1818–1820 near the Teatro Grande. It was owned by the first Count of Carvalhal, who had it refurbished after 1834. The last known performance there took place in 1838.

name: Capelas de Santa Isabel
notes: This entry describes two chapels dedicated to Saint Elizabeth. One is inside the Misericórdia building in Funchal, probably built in the early eighteenth century and noted for its gilded carved altar; the other is attached to the hospital of Santa Cruz.

name: Colégio e Igreja de São João Evangelista
notes: The Jesuit college and church of São João Evangelista in Funchal date from the Jesuits' arrival in 1570, with the building constructed in the seventeenth century. It was later used as a seminary, barracks and public offices, and the church was restored in 1847. The entry reproduces eighteenth-century descriptions of the chapels, their founders and benefactors.

candidates.name: Igreja de São João Evangelista do Colégio do Funchal

name: Rua da Princesa D. Maria Amelia
notes: Rua da Princesa D. Maria Amélia is a Funchal street named by the municipal council in 1852 to mark Princess Maria Amélia's visit to Madeira. It links Rua da Imperatriz D. Amélia with the area near the Pontinha.

candidates.name: Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amélia

name: Leite Monteiro
notes: Leite Monteiro Park is a public park at Monte, above Funchal. It was begun by the municipal council in 1894 and named after the council president, Dr José Leite Monteiro. It contains the marble Fonte de Nossa Senhora, whose 18th-century inscription records Charles Murray's purchase of its water.

name: Fortaleza de S. Tiago
notes: The Fortress of São Tiago stands on a rocky point east of Funchal harbour. It was built during the Philippine period (dated 1614) and later enlarged and rebuilt in 1767. It housed British gunners during the English occupation and, in 1921, a mountain artillery battery.

name: Aviceiro ou Fonte do Aviceiro
notes: Aviceiro, or Fonte do Aviceiro, is a locality in the parish of Santo António, near Lombo de D. Isabel. It lies on the road leading to Curral das Freiras.

name: Avenida do Doutor Jose Antonio de Almada
notes: The Avenida do Doutor José António de Almada is an avenue in Funchal named after Dr José António de Almada. Formerly the Pontinha road, it was built around 1874 along the coast south of the Vigias and Lambert quintas.
